title: Peter and Paul (29 June)
hook: the rock and the tentmaker, remembered on one day

segments.voice: Yesterday, bridegroom, and the best man who was glad to step back. Your line was I must decrease. Whose good work did you point to? Day one thousand forty-five.

A shared table in Antioch. Peter is eating with gentile believers. Then visitors arrive from James in Jerusalem, and Peter quietly pulls back and keeps himself apart. Paul sees it, and he doesn't take Peter aside for a private word. He writes about it later, in a letter, in the King James Bible: "But when Peter was come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed." Face to face, in front of everyone. Two leaders of the young church, disagreeing in public about who gets to sit at the table. And yet the church calendar puts the two of them on the same day, one feast, both names: not Peter's day and Paul's day, but both. Today, Peter and Paul.
screen: `WHO GETS TO SIT AT THE TABLE?`

segments.voice: Start with how different they were. Peter was a fisherman from Galilee named Simon. In John's Gospel, when his brother Andrew brings him to Jesus, Jesus gives him a new name on the spot: "thou shalt be called Cephas, which is by interpretation, A stone." Later, in Matthew: "thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church." Paul was a different kind of man entirely. He had hunted down Jesus's followers, until a blinding light on the road to Damascus turned him around. He wrote letters, crossed seas, argued in synagogues and marketplaces, and paid his own way with his hands. Acts says of him and his friends, "by their occupation they were tentmakers." The rock and the tentmaker. The one who walked Galilee with Jesus, and the one who met him on a road, after the resurrection. Now the word pillar. It comes from Paul himself, in the same letter where he tells of the row. He describes going up to Jerusalem, where "James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars," gave him "the right hands of fellowship." Shaking hands across a real difference: Peter to his own people, Paul to the gentiles. So the feast doesn't pretend they always agreed. It holds them up side by side, as two pillars holding up one roof. Churches read Peter's place differently. Catholic teaching sees the bishop of Rome as Peter's successor and reads the rock as Peter himself; Orthodox and Protestant Christians understand the rock and Peter's role in other ways. Tradition says both men died in Rome for their faith. And a letter that carries Peter's name calls Paul "our beloved brother."

Here's the practice: bring two different friends to mind. Settle, and breathe. Pick two people you love who are nothing alike. One loud, one quiet. One who plans, one who wings it. Maybe two who'd argue if you put them in a room. Hold the first one in mind, and what they give you that nobody else does. Then the second. If you pray, you can thank God for each of them by name. If you don't, just be grateful, one at a time, and notice how both of them hold up something in your life. The bell holds the time.
Cephas. The name Jesus gave Simon, meaning a stone, later called Peter, who together with Paul the tentmaker is remembered on one feast as two pillars.
Your line: two pillars. Today, tell one of those two different friends, in a message or out loud, one specific thing you're grateful for. Day one thousand forty-five.

howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox and some Anglican and Lutheran churches keep Peter and Paul together on one feast day, reading of Peter's confession and of Paul's ministry.

fork.setup: you're Paul in Antioch. Peter, a leader you respect, has pulled back from eating with gentile believers. what do you do?
options: withstand him to his face, in front of everyone.
fork.reveal: Paul confronts him publicly. yet in the same letter he tells of the right hands of fellowship, and the church remembers both on one day.

original.note: Greek: rock. "Upon this rock" is spoken to Peter, Petros.

trapdoor: what you thought: two saints who got along perfectly.
what it means: a fisherman and a tentmaker, very different and once at odds, remembered together on one feast.
what a scholar hears: the pillar image comes from Paul, who calls Cephas one of those "who seemed to be pillars" in the same letter as the row.
recall: mocked of the wise men, exceeding wroth

notes: 'Tradition says both men died in Rome for their faith' is attributed to tradition; no dates given.
Range of views on Peter's role and the rock (Catholic papal succession; Orthodox and Protestant readings) is compressed and unranked; confirm fair.
'A letter that carries Peter's name' avoids any authorship claim for 2 Peter; confirm.
Galatians 2:9 calls Cephas (not Paul) a pillar; the lesson says the 'two pillars' image for both is the feast's, and that the word comes from Paul; confirm framing.
howItsDone names which churches keep the joint feast; confirm 'some Anglican and Lutheran churches'.
Original: πέτρα (Matthew 16:18) with the Petros/petra wordplay mentioned only in the note; confirm.

Editor pass: hook now opens on the Antioch table rather than a KJV quotation plus 'That's Paul ... in the King James Bible' (the same opener as 1032, 1038 and the original 1040); 'visitors' now 'visitors from James' per Galatians 2:12. Teach no longer says Peter 'met Jesus on the shore' and was renamed 'on the spot' in the same breath, which mixed Mark's call by the sea with John 1:42; it now follows John (Andrew brings him). 'Walked the shore' became 'walked Galilee'.

Second editor pass: hook's 'one feast, one name' contradicted the screen head 'one feast, two names' and became 'one feast, both names'; 'Catholics see' became 'Catholic teaching sees' (no claim about every Catholic).
Audit pass: fixed a garbled teach line ('Catholic teaching sees ... and hear the rock').
